articles.title: Ratko Mladić: The monstrous crimes of the 'Butcher of Bosnia'
articles.summary: The Bosnian Serb commander led a campaign of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian conflict.
articles.body:
Ratko Mladić, who has died at the age of 84, was the bull-necked "Butcher of Bosnia".

As Commander of the Bosnian Serb army, he oversaw a brutal campaign of "ethnic cleansing" as Yugoslavia splintered in the 1990s.

The phrase was a chilling euphemism for the massacre of tens of thousands of men, women and children - in pursuit of what he saw as a chance to fulfil the historic destiny of Greater Serbia.

It was a goal he pursued with single-minded determination and studied brutality - and it made him responsible for the bloodiest atrocities Europe has witnessed since Hitler's Third Reich.

His fanaticism made him a hero to his people. He told them their Muslim neighbours planned to "impale Serbs, burn them alive, crucify them and put out their eyes".

He led the long and bloody siege of Sarajevo; killing and maiming its citizens in a daily hail of shells and sniper-fire.

When his troops overran the UN-declared safe area of Srebrenica, he promised they were safe. Later, 8,000 men and boys were led to unmarked graves.

He and his political counterpart, Radovan Karadžić, ripped Bosnia apart - committing acts of genocide and vicious crimes against humanity.

The barrel-chested warlord displayed no remorse, giving relatives of his victims a cheery thumbs-up at his eventual trial in the Hague.

"Borders are drawn in blood," he is reported to have said. "And states marked out with graves."

Ratko Mladić was born on 12 March 1942 in a small mountain village near Sarajevo, then part of the German-controlled Independent State of Croatia - although he always claimed to be a year younger.

Two years later, his father was killed fighting for Tito's partisans against Nazi-backed Croat nationalists.

Mladić was brought up in the new, post-war construct of Yugoslavia. After a short apprenticeship as a tinsmith, he chose a military career.

He graduated from officer school in 1965. Proving himself an ambitious and capable soldier, he rose rapidly through the ranks, commanding army units in Macedonia and Kosovo.

Tito's death in 1980 was the beginning of the end for Yugoslavia - always an uneasy confederation of opposing factions, competing nationalisms and simmering hatred.

In June 1991, Croatia declared independence. Mladić was sent in with the Yugoslav army in an effort to re-impose control.

He gained a reputation for courage bordering on recklessness, ever-present in frontline trenches and personally leading expeditions to clear mines.

His men loved him for it, their devotion bordering on religious.

As the war spilled over into Bosnia, his force switched uniforms - pledging support for the breakaway Republika Srpska.

He saw the Muslim population as invaders - the result of an ancient occupation by Ottoman Turks.

Mladić vowed to right what he considered a historical injustice, drive out the intruders and then build the ethnically pure nation of his dreams.

So began the siege of Sarajevo - the Bosnian capital defended by a rag-tag multi-ethnic force of Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims).

With his troops dug in on surrounding hillsides, the blockade lasted 1,425 days. It was the longest city siege in the savage history of modern warfare.

On 22 July 1993, nearly 4,000 shells rained down on its terrified people.

By the end of the siege, 13,000 were dead from shell-fire or a sniper's bullet; almost every building in the city either damaged or destroyed.

In the villages around the capital, legions of men were killed or carted off to prison camps; thousands of women were mercilessly raped.

A communiqué from Gen Mladić's headquarters captured his attitude. "Shoot at slow intervals until I order you to stop," it said.

"Target Muslim neighbourhoods - not many Serbs live there. Shell them until they are on the edge of madness."

Revelling in the power of his army, he gave orders by radio, the messages deliberately left unscrambled so they would be picked up and broadcast worldwide.

"Burn their brains," he screamed as his soldiers took aim at one enclave, telling them to follow his orders "as if given by God."

At weekends, he would visit his family, his wife and two children kept safe in Belgrade.

They would play board games, the conversation deliberately avoiding politics. But his 23-year-old daughter, Ana, had fallen in love with a young doctor and human rights activist.

The doctor gave her an ultimatum: renounce your father or never see me again.

Torn between dreams of love and bonds of family, Ana took her father's favourite gun from its display case. Moments later, she pulled the trigger.

Mladić struggled to come to terms with her suicide, preferring wild conspiracy theories which blamed the tragedy on everyone but himself.

It launched fighter attacks and cruise missile strikes on Mladić's positions around Sarajevo, most of them with devastating effect.

The siege was broken but his murderous campaign to cleanse the country was far from over.

That summer, tens of thousands of Bosniak civilians were gathered in Srebrenica: a small mountain town in eastern Bosnia.

They were under the protection of the United Nations, which had declared it a "safe area".

Bosnian Serb troops bombarded them with heavy shells and rockets. Five days later, Mladić strutted into town surrounded by TV camera crews.

In the main square, he handed out sweets, patted children on the head and assured them all would be fine. They were not fooled.

The handful of Dutch peacekeepers did nothing as men were shot and women were raped.

There followed the single most heinous act on European soil since World War Two.

Mladić's troops rounded up every Bosniak male they could find, marched them to remote sites and murdered them on an industrial scale.

In just a few days, 8,000 men and boys were tied up, blindfolded and shot. Some of them were as young as twelve, others in their late seventies.

All of them were cruelly pushed into mass, unmarked graves.

It was genocide: a black moment in European history and the UN's darkest hour.

It was a crime that took a high degree of organisation; the people had been promised UN protection and all this had happened right under its nose.

Later, the UN Secretary General, Kofi Annan, wrote that responsibility lay "first and foremost with those who planned and carried out the massacre". However, the international community had "made serious errors of judgement, rooted in a philosophy of impartiality", he added.

America offered $5m for information leading to his capture. A year later, Bosnian President Biljana Plavsic buckled to international pressure and dismissed him.

But it would be 14 years before he stood trial at the Hague.

He returned to Belgrade, enjoying the support and protection of President Slobodan Milošević.

Mladić lived openly; deer-hunting with friends, eating in swanky restaurants and even attending football matches.

He remained a hero to swathes of his countrymen, who saw in him the Serbian martial spirit and an echo of the past glories of their nation.

They were determined not to give him to an International Court. The president even established a military force dedicated to Mladić's personal protection.

The net began to tighten when, in October 2000, Slobodan Milošević was himself arrested and later delivered to the Hague.

International politics was beginning to bite, Serbia's entry to the European Union held up by its protection of the fugitives.

That night, Mladić fled; no longer guaranteed the sanctuary of his state.

He spent the next decade moving from safe-house to safe-house, first protected by a loyal team of bodyguards and, when they dwindled away, by his family.

In July 2008, his former political ally, Radovan Karadžić - now a long-bearded faith-healer - was arrested on a bus in Belgrade.

The new Serbian regime delivered him to the International Court, with which it had formalised co-operation. General Mladić was next.

The police tailed his children to a remote, squalid farmhouse where they stood alone in the courtyard for no apparent reason.

Too nervous to meet them, Mladić was watching through a window. When the security forces went in, they found a dishevelled 69-year-old man who had suffered several strokes.

The court sat for more than 500 days, heard from nearly 600 witnesses, and examined nearly 10,000 bits of evidence.

Due process was followed, although few doubted what the verdict would be.

Ratko Mladić was shown giving orders to his troops immediately before the Srebrenica massacre and convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the "customs of war".

He entered the courtroom with a smile and a thumbs-up to the cameras but exploded with anger at the verdicts.

Screaming that it was "all lies", he was forcibly removed. His sentence meant he would die in prison.

Among the many victims and their relatives present at his trial was Fikret Alic, a prisoner famously filmed in a skeletal state in a Bosnian Serb concentration camp in 1992.

"Justice has been done," he said. "The war criminal has been convicted". Others simply dissolved in tears.

But the widespread joy at the verdicts was far from universal.

Some Bosniaks were disappointed he had not been convicted of crimes outside Sarajevo and Srebrenica. And many fellow Serbs reacted with rage.

One leading politician in Republika Srpska condemned the trial as a plot to demonise his people, and called for them to "forever erase every mention" of the court proceedings from school history books.

In 2024, the court turned down his application to serve the rest of his sentence in Serbia. Having suffered heart attacks and strokes, Mladić claimed that his health would be better protected in his home country.

His lawyers continued to reapply unsuccessfully for his release, on the grounds that he had only months to live.

Both Serbia and Russia have supported his legal appeals. In Bosnia, by contrast, an opposition politician was sentenced to three years in prison for "glorifying" Karadžić and Mladić in January 2026.

For many of his people, the "Butcher of Bosnia" was just a simple soldier and the protector of their way of life. But he will be remembered by Bosniaks and most of the international community as a murderous thug who disgraced the European stage.

In Bosnia, Muslims and Serbs live side-by-side in uneasy cohabitation. The violent nationalist war waged by Mladić and Radovan Karadžić in the 1990s may be over, but tension still exists.

articles.title: 'Pak deployed spies to find S-400s': Top military official's explosive claim on Op Sindoor
articles.summary: Defence News: NEW DELHI: Pakistan deployed spies and activated sleeper cells inside India in an attempt to locate S-400 air defence systems during Operation Sindoor.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan deployed spies and activated sleeper cells inside India in an attempt to locate S-400 air defence systems during Operation Sindoor, Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra has claimed. He said that Islamabad used “every trick in the book” to identify the location of the systems.Mishra, in an interview with the news agency ANI, said Pakistan considered S-400 its biggest threat after repeated instances of Pakistani aerial assets being intercepted by the system. He claimed Pakistani efforts to locate the air defence systems involved satellite support from other countries, air intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities.“They had deployed spies within our country, activated their sleeper cell within our country to find out where the S-400 is,” Mishra said, while describing Pakistan's efforts to track the system during the conflict.He also indicated that Islamabad may have received satellite assistance from another country, but declined to name it.“They were using satellite help from other nations. I don't want to use the name of the country,” Mishra said.Mishra added that the Adampur Air Force Station came under particularly heavy attack because Pakistan believed it was associated with the deployment of India's S-400 systems.During Operation Sindoor, the S-400 demonstrated its long-range strike capability by bringing down a large Pakistani aircraft at a distance of more than 300 km, according to the Air Force. The system was also credited with engaging multiple aerial threats during the hostilities.With the delivery of fourth S-400 system, the Air Force has expanded the geographical area covered by the air-defence network, further strengthening its ability to protect critical military and strategic assets.The S-400's combination of long-range detection, multiple interceptor options and ability to engage different categories of aerial threats makes it one of the most important components of India's layered air-defence system.

articles.title: CaseOh began streaming in 2022 after being laid off from a maintenance job; two years later, he was accepting one of gaming's biggest creator awards
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Case Dylan Baker, better known as CaseOh, did not start his creator career with a huge audience waiting for him. His early life was much more ordinary.
articles.body: Case Dylan Baker, better known as CaseOh, did not start his creator career with a huge audience waiting for him. His early life was much more ordinary. He worked regular jobs, including full-time maintenance and grass-mowing work alongside his father in rural Arkansas. The job was not exactly easy. He later described the work as exhausting and grueling, while money was tight enough that his bank card was once declined at a Family Dollar store. The strange part is how quickly everything changed after he finally gave streaming a serious shot. His mother, Angie Baker, had already watched him play games casually and became one of his earliest supporters. She saw the humor in him and pushed him to treat streaming like a real career. He already had basic gaming gear, so Baker decided to take the gamble.CaseOh built his first audience before he even went liveHis first big move was not a Twitch stream. It was TikTok. On September 10, 2022, Baker spent hours recording and editing NBA 2K23 gameplay clips. Then he uploaded 22 videos in one day. That strategy worked almost immediately. More than 10,000 people followed him overnight.So when he finally went live on Twitch on September 11, he was not starting from zero. Around 126 concurrent viewers were already there.The growth kept moving at a ridiculous pace. Within weeks, his streaming income had passed what he was making from his day job. Baker then made a deal with his chat. Reach 5,000 active Twitch subscribers, and he would leave maintenance behind for good. He hit the target and became a full-time creator. His mother later quit her own job to become his business manager.His streams became bigger because CaseOh made the joke part of the showCaseOh did not stay locked into NBA 2K23. He moved into indie simulators, horror games like Five Nights at Freddy’s and Granny, plus Roblox.But the games were only part of the appeal. His chat became another character in every stream.Viewers regularly roasted him with food-based jokes and nicknames such as “built like a 1x1 Lego piece” and “Case-a-dilla.” Instead of shutting the jokes down, Baker leaned into the chaos. His fake anger and dramatic chat bans became recurring meme material on TikTok and YouTube Shorts.That interaction helped create the community around his streams. He usually broadcasts for around four hours a night from a modest setup. Early on, he even had to rely on an unstable mobile hotspot because of poor rural internet in Arkansas. He has also turned down multi-million-dollar deals when he felt the games would not entertain his audience.In 2024, the story reached The Game Awards stageBy December 2024, the creator who had started with lawn mowing and maintenance work was standing inside Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater.CaseOh won Content Creator of the Year at The Game Awards 2024, beating names including Usada Pekora, Typical Gamer and Techno Gamerz. He also won Best Variety Streamer at The Streamer Awards.His streams have since reached peak audiences close to 300,000 concurrent viewers. What makes the rise wild is the timing: less than 27 months after his first TikTok upload, Baker had gone from a modest working life in Arkansas to accepting one of gaming’s biggest creator awards.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Supreme Court asked to rule on dispute over Sturgeon inquiry documents
articles.summary: Scotland's information commissioner wants to challenge the Scottish government's use of exemptions to block the release of information.
articles.body:
The UK's Supreme Court is being asked to rule on the Scottish government's refusal to release documents linked to an inquiry that cleared Nicola Sturgeon of breaching the ministerial code.

Ministers have cited legal professional privilege as grounds for refusing a freedom of information (FOI) request from a member of the public.

Benjamin Harrop was seeking internal emails, messages and other communications about whether the government had a legal right to withhold the material.

The Court of Session later overturned a ruling by Information Commissioner David Hamilton that the documents should be released, but Hamilton is now seeking permission to take the case to the UK's highest court.

Scotland's FOI law allows some information requests to be refused if they would compromise confidential communications between lawyers and their clients - but it is subject to a public interest test.

Hamilton said he was worried that the Court of Session ruling had wider implications, making it too difficult to obtain legally-privileged documents.

He said: "It is my view that this ruling runs contrary to the parliament's clear intention behind the FOI Act."

"There are significant implications and risks placed on the public's right to access information because of this ruling – it is therefore clearly in the public interest that I seek to challenge this at the Supreme Court".

A Scottish government spokesperson said: "As this is subject to live litigation in would not be appropriate to comment."

The row can ultimately be traced back to the bitter dispute between Nicola Sturgeon and the late Alex Salmond over the government's handling of harassment complaints against him.

Salmond, a former SNP leader and first minister, challenged the way the investigation was conducted, and in 2019 government lawyers conceded the process had been unlawful and procedurally unfair .

The fallout triggered allegations that Sturgeon had breached the ministerial code through her handling of contacts with Salmond and by misleading the Scottish Parliament about what she knew and when.

The government's independent adviser on the ministerial code, Irish barrister James Hamilton KC, carried out an investigation and concluded in 2021 that Sturgeon had not breached the code .

In a separate criminal case, Salmond was cleared in 2020 of sexually assaulting nine women.

Harrop, who has said he joined the SNP in 2014, has written on the Wings Over Scotland website about his efforts to obtain information, claiming the Scottish government has a "pathological aversion to transparency and accountability".

The particular information request that could potentially trigger a Supreme Court ruling asks for material relating to the internal discussions among ministers, advisers and civil servants about whether they could claim an FOI exemption for material gathered by James Hamilton.

While some information was divulged, the government claimed legal privilege over some of the correspondence, with the Court of Session eventually ruling those did not have to be disclosed.

Scottish Labour's acting leader Jackie Baillie claimed that too often "the SNP operates under a cloak of secrecy".

She added: "This legal challenge could have significant implications for the disclosure of information.

"However, it should not take lengthy legal disputes to get answers from the SNP government.

"We need to see an end to the culture of cover-up that the SNP has created and a renewed commitment to openness and integrity in government."

Before his death from a heart attack in October 2024, Salmond was pursuing a separate civil case against the Scottish government, seeking damages arising from unlawful handling of complaints against him.

A millionaire businessman and former rock musician Paul McManus has since taken over the legal rights of that case and has said he will continue the action.

articles.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
articles.summary: Police have arrested a 19-year-old male suspect after an incident in which two people were killed near the German capital.
articles.body:
Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said.

Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used.

It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school.

One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported.

The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported.

Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide".

"The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger.

"I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said.

State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence".

The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday.

Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come.

"We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said.

A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added.

Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany.

articles.title: Ex-ICE agent charged over shooting is freed by Texas authorities
articles.summary: Christian Castro, accused of carrying out nonfatal shooting in Minnesota, walks free after extradition lapse.
articles.body:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged with shooting a Venezuelan man and allegedly lying about it during an immigration raid in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail a day after a federal judge refused to order his return to the US state of Minnesota.

The former ICE agent, Christian Castro, had been detained in a county jail in Texas since May, charged in connection with the nonfatal shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis and hitting him in the leg when firing through the front door of his home during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota on January 14.

The immigration sweep was part of a mass deportation effort under United States President Donald Trump. Prosecutors said Castro wrongfully accused Sosa-Celis and another man of assaulting an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

Castro was freed on Thursday morning from the Carrizales-Rucker Cameron County Detention Center near Brownsville, Texas, a city on the US border with Mexico. A Minnesota judge had issued a nationwide warrant for his arrest in May. Minnesota officials and the state’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension eventually detained him in Texas on May 29. Minnesota authorities then sought his extradition.

Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for more than 90 days. At that point, the suspect must either be transferred or released. The deadline for Castro expired on Thursday.

Upon exiting the detention centre, Castro motioned towards a few camera operators and a reporter crowding around him and quickly got into an SUV that drove off.

In a ruling on Wednesday, District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr wrote that he could not intervene or prevent a county sheriff from releasing Castro given that Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and close political ally of Trump, had refused to sign the extradition warrant for political reasons. Abbott argued that he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a “fugitive” under the Extradition Clause, lawyers for the state of Texas said.

The governor also said last week that he would not respond to the extradition request, citing ongoing investigations into alleged fraud in Minnesota’s social service programmes, which Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week to block Castro’s anticipated release. He also sued Abbott to try to force his hand at signing the extradition warrant.

Ellison said Abbott’s inaction unlawfully sidestepped federal extradition to bolster Trump’s deportation campaign. He declared that legal proceedings would persist but omitted specifying what those future actions would entail.

Beginning in December, Trump orchestrated a large-scale deployment of federal agents to Minnesota. The operation lasted less than three months and fuelled protests and allegations of civil liberties violations from residents and watchdog groups. Two US citizens were killed by federal agents during the operation.

Minnesota officials have warned that Castro may flee the US if released, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico.

During those calls, Castro talked “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released”, according to Minnesota’s lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could indeed flee the country but added that “the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication”.

articles.title: Obituary: Ratko Mladic, war criminal convicted of Srebrenica genocide, dies
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic a Bosnian Serb war criminal, has died in prison aged 84.
articles.body:
Ratko Mladic, a war criminal convicted over the first genocide on European soil since the second world war, has died prison in The Hague at the age of 84.

Earlier this year, Serbia requested that Mladic be allowed to receive medical treatment outside prison, saying his health condition was “serious” and that he “required serious medical treatment”.

The United Nations International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said that Mladic was receiving adequate medical care while in detention.

Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia”, Mladic was one of the best-known and most notorious military commanders of the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia.

International courts convicted him of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the 1992–1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was sentenced to life in prison

The most notorious part of his criminal legacy is linked to the genocide in Srebrenica, in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, near the border with Serbia.

Bosnian Serb forces under Mladic’s command seized Srebrenica in July 1995, despite the UN declaring the municipality a “safe area”. After the enclave fell, more than 8,000 Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) men and boys were killed by Mladic’s forces in the days that followed.

Some of the civilians were captured and executed at locations in and around Srebrenica. Others were killed after attempting to flee through the forests towards territory controlled by the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The bodies of victims were later discovered in numerous mass graves, while many were identified years after the war. The remains of around 1,000 victims are still being sought. International courts established that the killings constituted genocide.

Srebrenica has remained a symbol of one of the gravest crimes committed in Europe since the second world war.

From the Yugoslav army to commander of the army of Republika Srpska

Mladic was born in the village of Bozanovici near Kalinovik, about 40km (25 miles) south of Sarajevo.

He began his military career in the Yugoslav People’s army and gradually rose through the military’s command structure.

When Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence from Yugoslavia in the spring of 1992, following Slovenia and Croatia, Bosnian Serbs established their own political and military structures and proclaimed Republika Srpska, which controlled territory covering roughly half of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

In May 1992, Mladic was appointed commander of the Republika Srpska’s army. Over the next three and a half years, he sought to seize parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled by the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the capital Sarajevo, devastating areas in his path. However, his forces failed to achieve major territorial gains in several key areas.

The political and military leadership of Republika Srpska sought to separate Serb-controlled territories from Bosnia and Herzegovina and create a separate, territorially contiguous Serb state within the country. Republika Srpska would formally become one of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s two entities under the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement.

Mladic’s forces were involved in a large number of atrocities across Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In addition to the Srebrenica genocide, international courts found Mladic responsible for a campaign of terror against Sarajevo’s civilian population, the hostage-taking of UN peacekeepers and other crimes.

Sarajevo was surrounded by Bosnian Serb forces for almost 44 months. From positions on the surrounding hills, they shelled the city and used snipers against its residents.

More than 11,500 people from all ethnic groups were killed, while many others were wounded or displaced.

The Sarajevo Siege, which Mladic directed, became one of the defining episodes of the Bosnian war and one of the longest sieges of a capital city in modern history.

After the war ended in 1995, Mladic evaded arrest and spent almost 16 years in hiding. He became one of Europe’s most wanted fugitives accused of war crimes.

He was arrested in Serbia in May 2011 in the village of Lazarevo, near Zrenjanin, at the home of a relative. Several days later, he was transferred to The Hague, where his trial began before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

His arrest was one of the key conditions set by the international community for Serbia’s progress towards closer relations with the European Union. Belgrade faced political and financial pressure from Western countries to cooperate with the tribunal and transfer Mladic to The Hague.

In 2017, the tribunal sentenced him to life imprisonment. The courts established his individual criminal responsibility for a number of crimes.

Although his convictions were final, Mladic continues to have support among sections of the Serbian public and political circles in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In Banja Luka, Belgrade and other areas with predominantly Serb populations, murals depicting him can still be seen. Some members of the public continue to portray him as a military hero rather than a convicted war criminal.

That attitude towards Mladic is part of a broader problem of confronting the legacy of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. While international courts have established facts concerning the genocide and other crimes, political and social divisions over the country’s wartime past remain deeply entrenched.

Denial of the Srebrenica genocide and the glorification of convicted war criminals remain serious problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

According to data from the Srebrenica Memorial Centre, 149 cases of public denial of the Srebrenica genocide were recorded during the first quarter of 2026, including statements by public figures. That represents an increase compared with 2025, when 99 such cases were recorded.

The UN General Assembly adopted a resolution in May 2024 establishing July 11 as the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica.

The resolution was intended to preserve the memory of the victims and promote a culture of remembrance, while also reaffirming the importance of confronting genocide denial and preventing the recurrence of such crimes.

articles.title: Survivor's Christian Hubicki marvels at China's robotics games records: 'Willing to break the robots to do it'
articles.summary: The World Humanoid Robot Games' crashes show how far the technology still needs to go to be useful, "Survivor" reality TV star and robotics scientist Christian Hubicki says.
articles.body: The World Humanoid Robot Games made headlines this week, putting robotics experts in awe and leaving social media scrollers laughing at the robots’ histrionics, viral stumbles, and dramatic crashes and burns. In its second year, it is making an annual event out of stress-testing the limits of technological advancement, while allaying fears to the public that SkyNet is not on the verge of taking over the world. "The goal of this event really was to show how fast we can get robots to go," Christian Hubicki, Florida State University mechanical-engineering professor and robotics lab director, told Fox News Digital on the final day of the five-day event. "What happens to them afterwards? Well, as we can see, it's a bit dramatic. "They didn't care so much how they stopped. In fact, they had this big wall that they just smashed into." LET'S LOOK BACK ON THE BEST MOMENTS (READ: CRASHES) FROM THE WORLD HUMANOID ROBOT GAMES The robots might be running faster than Usain Bolt before they know how to stop, but the tech is still at the stage of standing up from a crawl, according to Hubicki, who is also known for being a past contestant on the CBS reality TV show "Survivor." "They wanted to break the record, and they're willing to break the robots to do it," Hubicki said. "You can see robots are sparking, limbs are flying off. It's incredibly kinetic. It's like these things are almost like missiles flying at this wall. All to break the record." The record broken was Bolt's 9.58 seconds in the 100-meter dash, but in a show of just how fast the robots can go and technology can advance, Saturday's 9.39 mark only lasted a few days. A Chinese humanoid robot – Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre – on the event's final day won the large-size robot 100-meter final at 8.64 seconds, almost a second faster than Bolt's human world-record time. CHINESE MARATHON ROBOT FALLS, BREAK DANCES ITSELF TO PIECES "This is a major milestone that people who work in specifically legged robotics, like I do, have wanted to see for a long time – just to prove that we could do this," Hubicki said. "So this is big deal. I watched this. This is incredible, how fast they get these robots to go. "At the same time, we're not terribly surprised. We've known for a while that motors and gears and joints of robots could outperform people. We've known this. There have been papers specifically published that are titled, 'Why Robots Don't Outrun People Yet.' And the answer was we've just got to make them just a little bit smarter." Artificial intelligence is helping, but the games also show how far the technology remains from reliable, practical use. CHINESE HUMANOID ROBOT BREAKS USAIN BOLT'S 100M DASH RECORD AT 9.39 SECONDS "There's still a lot of human intelligence built into how these things are moving around," Hubicki said. "They're being told exactly what to do, go forward, rotate around the course, right? The higher level intelligence, we would say, is still very limited. And you can see this in the other events as well. "You can see when they're playing robot tennis – and by the way, I'm very impressed with what they've been able to accomplish – they had to have these sort of external cameras pointing out exactly where the ball is so they know where to hit the ball. And that's OK, it's work in progress," he said. "There's still a lot of limited intelligence on the robots, but of course they are getting better." As in human athletics, the 100 meters was one of the highlights of the Beijing games, underscoring advances in robot mobility, balance and control systems. NEW AI BRAIN LETS ROBOTS MOVE LIKE HUMANS "The organizers of this event did a great job of highlighting specifically the types of tasks that Chinese robotics companies are great at doing, which are the athletic events," Hubicki said. "They focus a lot on robots that do these fantastic athletic stunts." "And you might be wondering, couldn't robots already go faster than people? Well, yes, wheeled robots absolutely could," he explained. "We have had RC cars that outpace people for a very long time. But the challenge with humanoids has been coordinating all the motors, all the joints. "We are so good at this as people, but thanks to the AI boom of the last handful of years, we figured out smarter and smarter ways to make robots coordinate their motion so they don't fall down while moving faster and faster, and squeeze out every last bit of performance that you can out of the motors – and that's why we're starting to see faster and faster robots." The event, dubbed the "Robot Olympics," brought together more than 2,000 robots from 666 teams, most of them Chinese. Its 51 disciplines included sports contests as well as task-based challenges in simulated factories, restaurants, offices and emergency settings. ROBOT SOCCER PLAYER DENTS WALL WITH TERRIFYING KICKS "They are getting smarter," he said. "The challenge is to get them smarter in a way that is really practical for us. I mean, it's fun for me to watch a robot going Usain Bolt speeds down a runway, but it doesn't really help us too much. The real challenge is how can we get them to be reliable and practical to help us." Step one was to make them run as fast as they can – and look good doing it – before they knew how to stop. "Last year's robots looked a little stiff and uncoordinated," Niu, 34, told Reuters. "This year, they are much better. They are like healthy newborn babies growing up." UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES Eventually, the tech will require getting them to think for themselves about how to stop. "The thing that's important to say about the smarts is it's a very specific kind of smarts – they're only figuring out how to coordinate their motion to the point where these robots, when they're running around, they don't even remember what happened a second ago," Hubicki said. "All they're looking at is like, 'Right now, what do I need to do to keep moving forward?'" "And so I think it's important for people to realize that when we see something that kind of moves like a duck, quacks like a duck, like a person here, it's not actually thinking like a duck in this particular case – it's very purpose-built, specific intelligence to keep this thing running and boy does it go fast. It's incredible." The kinetic robots will eventually have AI processing added in. AI BUILDS VIRTUAL HOMES WHERE ROBOTS LEARN FROM THEIR MISTAKES "The AI of these robots is so much simpler than what you would experience interacting with like a chatbot or Chat GPT," according to Hubicki. "It frankly doesn't need to. It would take too long on the computer to think as hard as those things. They just have to go quick, quick, quick, quick. So it's very simple. It's just saying, 'Hey, what's my pose? How fast am I moving? Where do I put my leg?' That's it." The intelligence tech still is artificial and just not "reliable" yet, Hubicki warned, as anyone who has seen the "nonsense" AI can sometimes produce. "You'll use some of these tools and it'll come up with something like, 'Wow, that's actually pretty brilliant,' and sometimes you're like, ‘Wait a second, that is nonsense,’ and it's only as good as you can verify," he said. "That's why it's not a particularly good fit right now to put on a robot – not because it's going to be coming up with some kind diabolical scheme but it just doesn't understand reality in the same way that we do." HUMANOID ROBOT SKIN SENSES PEOPLE BEFORE CONTACT Hubicki pointed to a viral social media video of a humanoid robot that looked like it went rogue. "We do see what happens when you put these robots in the real world," he said. "There was one of these humanoids, it just went and just kicked a kid in the stomach, and it didn't know the kid was there. "It wasn't even using the cameras. It's just interacting in a complicated world it doesn't even understand. So that's where a lot of the work has to go in order to actually have robots be able to interact with us in a way that is useful and helpful. Otherwise, you know, it's just a bull in a china shop." Recently, there was a New York Times report of Russia using AI-guided drones that killed three civilians in Ukraine, leading a Ukrainian military leader to warn that "we will be living in a 'Terminator' movie" before long. HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT "Certainly there's a lot of people, certainly governments are looking for all kinds of applications of AI and robotics, and that includes the battlefield," Hubicki said. "The war in Ukraine right now, it's a drone war. And I mean people talk about humanoid robots right now on the battlefield, there are unmanned aerial vehicles, little quadcopter drones that are just everywhere. And it's a brave new world. articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's order comes after the trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.

Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.

He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, noting in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever."

When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

It also led to a dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.

In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

There is no universally recognized international body setting the names of international waters. While the US president has broad discretion over how his country officially recognises landmarks, other countries do not have to follow.

Trump's latest order directs the US Department of the Interior to update the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US - to reflect the name change, the president said.

Canada, however, does not have to recognise name changes made by other countries and officials dismissed the idea in remarks earlier this week.

"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," said Industry Minister Melanie Joly on Tuesday.

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.

Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it wasn't a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade".

Trump said he'd been thinking about renaming the lake "for a long time".

"So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," Trump said.

"Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

The name change request comes amid a trade dispute that has seen US-Canada relations fall to new lows, with insults thrown back-and-forth between the Trump administration and Canadian officials over the past week.

There was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table sometime in the future.

Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said in a post on X that the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French "and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future US trade actions".

"We look forward to further constructive US clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty".

Trade talks collapsed at the last minute late on Friday night, with both sides accusing the other of demanding last-minute changes to a tentative deal.

articles.title: Man, 86, reunited with backpack 60 years after abandoning it during hiking accident
articles.summary: An 86-year-old Austrian man has been reunited with climbing equipment he was forced to abandon in a glacier crevasse more than six decades ago, after melting ice brought the long-lost belongings back to the surface.
articles.body: An 86-year-old Austrian man has been reunited with climbing equipment he was forced to abandon in a glacier crevasse more than six decades ago, after melting ice brought the long-lost belongings back to the surface. A hiker discovered the backpack on the Sulztalferner glacier in Austria’s western Tyrol region last month, at nearly 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) above sea level, according to Austrian police. Inside was a collection of items that had been preserved in the ice for decades, including an ice axe, camera, whistle and weathered document folder. Police officers investigated the discovery to see if the rucksack was evidence of a long-ago mountaineering accident. They were able to make out the owner’s name among the documents found inside, leading to his identification. Investigators learned that the man had lost the equipment during a climbing trip across the glacier in August 1963. He had fallen into a crevasse while roped together with several companions, police said. The others managed to pull him to safety, but he discarded his backpack in an effort to reduce his weight. Sixty-three years later, the lost equipment was finally returned. The man, who has not been publicly named, was unable to collect the belongings himself because of ill health, police said, and the items were instead returned to him through his son. The man’s son expressed his gratitude at the backpack’s return, according to a statement from Tirol police. It comes as alpine and global glaciers are shrinking as the world heats up. By the middle of the century, the number of glaciers disappearing is set to peak at up to 4,000 a year, if humans keep pumping out climate pollution, according to a study published last year. This is not the first time that objects – and even corpses – have been uncovered due to melting ice. In 1991, hikers in the Italian Alps discovered the mummified body of Ötzi the Iceman, who died 5,300 years ago.

articles.title: Indian-origin grandmother with Green Card allowed to leave ICE detention but her immigration case continues. DHS calls her flight risk
articles.summary: US News: Venkata Vasamsetty, the Indian-origin grandmother who has been living in the US for decades with a Green Card and has a house in North Carolina, two U.
articles.body: Venkata Vasamsetty, the Indian-origin grandmother who has been living in the US for decades with a Green Card and has a house in North Carolina, two US citizen daughters and US-born grandchildren, was granted bail after her ICE detention. But the immigration case is not solved. Vasamsetty was detained by ICE in August during an immigration check-in. The issue arose after Vasamsetty traveled to India during the Covid pandemic and stayed in India for over six months as she got Covid and had to be hospitalized. On her return to the US, it was flagged that she had overstayed in India and that a legal case was going on.Her family claimed that she won the legal case as it was proved that Vasamsetty did not intend to abandon her residency in the US by her overstay in India. But she was still called for her immigration check-in on August 11, when she was detained.Not a danger to the community but poses flight riskDuring Tuesday's bond hearing, Department of Homeland Security attorney Abby Cannon said Vasamsetty was not a danger to the community but she posed a significant flight risk. The DHS cited Vasamsetty's travel history between the United States and India, telling the judge that she spent 61 days in the United States in 2019, 96 days in 2021 and 67 days in 2022. A Green Card holder is required to reside in the US for six months.DHS argued that her time abroad raised questions about whether she maintained her permanent residency and demonstrated an ability to leave the country again.Vasamsetty's attorney, Helen Parsonage, argued that these trips were mostly for caring her aging parents, including her father before his death. Vasamsetty's family also said they are disputing her travel dates overall, arguing that no exact timetable was brought in or agreed to as evidence to explain how they arrived at the numbers they did, ABC11 reported.Parsonage argues that Vasamsetty was unlikely to flee and she never missed an immigration court appearance or ICE check-in in her earlier removal case. He also said that Vasamsetty did not have any criminal history.Judge Chad Bayse agreed that Vasamsetty's history of compliance weighed heavily in the decision. He found that DHS had not met its burden of proving that she would flee if released. Bayse pointed to Vasamsetty's long-standing ties to the United States, including her husband, two US-citizen daughters, grandchildren, a home, tax returns dating back to at least 2012, business ties, and her work as an elementary school substitute teacher. The judge did find that some flight risk exists because Vasamsetty has the resources and history to travel internationally. So he denied the request for the minimum bond and set bail at $7,500.Conditions for Vasamsetty's releaseVasamsetty must appear at all future court dates, comply with court orders and avoid arrests, illegal drugs and harmful contact with others.DHS has the right to appeal the bond decision. articles.title: Sports Direct's Ashley attacks Burnham over 'populist' High Street revival plans
articles.summary: In a letter, the entrepreneur accuses the prime minister of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons" with his latest cost of living and retail policies.
articles.body:
Billionaire Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley has criticised recent cost of living and retail policies from Andy Burnham as "populist reactions".

In a letter to the prime minister, the entrepreneur accused him of "jumping on 'everyday fixes' or bandwagons", while "disastrous" business rates policies and increases to the cost of employing workers were causing businesses to struggle.

He also described a previous proposal of increasing business rates on large warehouses to help reduce them for pubs and clubs as "delusional".

A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham would "build a new economy that backs British business, delivers growth in every postcode and ensures the essentials in life - like energy, water and housing - are affordable again."

Promises including cutting VAT from household electricity bills and reducing business rates for some firms is "just the start", they added.

He also brought forward a plan to end subscription traps and ban shops using misleading recommended retail prices, which can make it seem like discounts are larger than they really are.

In Ashley's letter, seen by the BBC and first reported by the Financial Times, he hit out at announcements made since Burnham succeeded Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.

The businessman called on Burnham to use his first Budget, scheduled for 27 October, to lower costs for employers and change the government's position on business rates.

Pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% business rates cut from April, while a review has been launched into how the tax, which high street firms have long called for reform to, is calculated.

"Shortsighted or populist reactions to underlying business challenges are not the answer," Ashley said in the letter.

Ashley has repeatedly called for a fundamental overhaul of the tax, including levelling the playing field between High Street retailers and online rivals.

"If your answer is to tax larger retailers even more, through hiking business rates on retailer owned or third-party warehouses whilst reducing rates for pubs and clubs, then that is simply delusional," he wrote.

Burnham previously said before he was prime minister that cuts for pubs, clubs and music venues could be paid for by higher levies on warehouses operated by online firms such as Amazon, and targeting the owners of empty high street properties.

Ashley built Frasers Group from a single Sports Direct store in Maidenhead in 1982 to a sprawling empire of dozens of brands employing 30,000 people.

The billionaire has frequently attracted controversy from investors and the media, with accusations over the years of building success by exploiting workers.

In 2016, Ashley admitted to MPs that workers at his Derbyshire warehouse had been paid below the minimum wage and a policy of fining staff for being late was unacceptable.

The business, still owned by Ashley but run by his son-in-law Michael Murray, this month bought luxury department store Harvey Nichols and promised a "significant restructuring" of the business.

Ashley also used his letter to ask Burnham how the prime minister intends to revive Harvey Nichols, which has faced financial challenges in recent years.

Referencing comments by Tory peer and former Marks & Spencer boss Lord Rose, who called the announcements "hot air", Ashley said "I agree with him".

"It is the disastrous business rates position (which I have raised many times over the years) and the dramatically increasing cost of employing people that are really causing business to struggle," Ashley said.

"You have the chance to make a difference or get it horribly wrong," he added.

Ashley said the High Street will be "further devastated" without major reforms, and warned Burnham's suggestion he will consider further business rates changes in the coming Budget are "too little, too late".

He also used the letter to attack Burnham's plans to clamp down on the use of recommended retail prices, saying instead the real issue is "price fixing in sporting goods and other markets" - where he cited the rising cost of official football merchandise.
